title: Open-Ring Enhancement in Pseudotumoral Multiple Sclerosis: Important Radiological Aspect
case_prompt: A 55-year-old woman with a remote history of ovarian cancer and no recent vaccinations or infections reported a one-month history of fatigue, mild bilateral retroorbital discomfort, and progressive visual loss—first in the right eye, then the left. On examination she had a right homonymous hemianopia and tetrahyperreflexia. Vital signs were normal. Laboratory tests including routine blood work were unremarkable. A brain MRI revealed a single 3.7 × 2.4 × 1.8 cm expansile lesion in the left temporo-occipital region extending into the splenium of the corpus callosum. On T1-weighted images the lesion was hypointense; on T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences it was hyperintense. There was significant perilesional vasogenic edema and no diffusion restriction. After contrast administration, there was peripheral enhancement in an open-ring configuration, with the incomplete portion directed toward the cortex.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. High-grade glioma was considered because of the mass effect, vasogenic edema, and midline extension — “The radiological characteristics were primarily those of high-grade glioma: an expansive lesion with important vasogenic edema and involvement of the corpus callosum that exceeded the midline.” It was deemed less likely because malignant lesions usually show a complete, irregular ring enhancement rather than an open ring — “Typically, ring enhancement is complete in abscesses and cancer; however, in the former, it is smooth and thin, while in the latter, it is thick and irregular.”
2. Primary CNS lymphoma was considered alongside glioblastoma due to similar imaging features — “Given the possibility of a primary tumor (glioblastoma, lymphoma)…”. It was argued against by the marked reduction in perfusion typical of demyelination, which is slower than in lymphomas — “marked reduction in blood flow perfusion compared with normal white matter, which flows slower than in abscesses, lymphomas, and high-grade gliomas.”
3. Metastasis was considered due to the patient’s history of ovarian cancer — “Despite the risk of metastasis because of the previous history of ovarian cancer (metastases do not possess a typical radiological pattern)…”. The imaging features were more characteristic of a primary neoplasm rather than multiple small metastatic foci.
4. Abscess was included in the initial differential as an infectious etiology — “mimics other tumor-like lesions, including neoplasms (gliomas, lymphomas), infections (abscesses, parasitic cysts)…”. It was less likely given the absence of diffusion restriction, since abscesses typically restrict — “…and unrestricted diffusion.”
5. Parasitic cysts were mentioned as rare mimics of tumefactive lesions — “mimics… infections (abscesses, parasitic cysts)…”. They were considered unlikely in the absence of epidemiologic risk factors and typical diffusion or cystic features.
6. Cerebral infarction can mimic tumefactive demyelination on histology when macrophages are abundant and was noted as a potential pitfall — “tissue samples from the center of the lesion, due to the presence of a large number of macrophages, can be misdiagnosed as cerebral infarction, unless staining for myelin and axon is performed.” Imaging without necrosis or typical vascular territory helped exclude infarction.
7. Pseudotumoral demyelinating disease was suspected because of the open-ring enhancement, which is highly specific for demyelination — “open-ring enhancement… alerted us to the possibility of demyelination…”.
